description.text: Gaius Julius Caesar, born in 100 BC, rose from a modest patrician background to become one of Rome’s most powerful generals, statesmen, and authors. He led the Roman armies through the Gallic Wars, defeating Pompey in the civil war, and was named dictator perpetuo in 44 BC, a title that paved the way for the collapse of the Roman Republic and the emergence of the Empire.

Caesar’s reforms reshaped Roman society: he introduced the Julian calendar, expanded citizenship, increased the Senate’s size, and enacted land and grain policies that altered the political landscape. His assassination on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC, triggered a chain of civil wars that ultimately led to the rise of Augustus and the imperial system that would dominate Europe for centuries.

curiosities.text: Caesar famously built a temporary bridge across the Rhine River in 55 BC, demonstrating Roman engineering prowess and asserting control over the frontier.
He was the first living Roman to have his portrait minted on coins, a symbolic gesture that foreshadowed the imperial cult of later emperors.
His death on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC, was the result of a conspiracy by senators who feared his growing power and the possibility of him becoming king.
